explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The verse says 22,600 of Tola's descendants were numbered in their genealogies as mighty men of valor in the days of David, Israel's king. That's a whole stadium of strong folks from one family. I'd hate to be the guy picking teams against them.

Moses, Israel's leader, doesn't show up in this verse at all. The text says the count happened "In the days of David," so that's the time to hold onto. Easy to mix up when you're flipping through old names. I once mixed up two pans in the dark, so I'm not judging.

Solomon, David's son (2 Samuel 12:24), is a good guess, since he comes right after David. But the verse names David's days for this count. Same family, one generation off. Close, friend, and no crumbs lost.

Not quite, friend. The verse never says a word about hiring soldiers from other lands. It says they had 36,000 troops for battle "for they had many wives and children." The army came from their own big family. No recruiting needed, just a lot of family dinners.

Right, friend. The text gives the reason in plain words: "for they had many wives and children." Nobody was hired from outside. The 36,000 troops grew right out of that household. That's a family reunion with a draft number.

That's right. The text says, "Their father Ephraim mourned for many days, and his relatives came to comfort him." Ezer and Elead were his sons, and he grieved them. I like that the family showed up for him. Nobody fixed it, they just came. That's what comfort looks like.

This one is true, friend. After Ezer and Elead were killed, the text says, "Their father Ephraim mourned for many days, and his relatives came to comfort him." The list of names stops and makes room for a father's grief. I think that's a gentle thing for a long list to do. It's a heavy part, so let's let it be heavy.

Yes. The verse says Ephraim named him Beriah "because tragedy had come upon his house." The name carries the memory of what his family went through. I think it shows that he didn't pretend the hurt wasn't there. The Bible keeps it real, friend.

That's a sweet guess, friend, and it would suit a newborn. But the text says the name came "because tragedy had come upon his house." The name looks back at what the family had lost. A new baby, yes, but the name remembers the hard part.

Peace is a lovely word for a baby, friend. But the verse says Ephraim named him Beriah "because tragedy had come upon his house." So the name points back at the grief, not at calm. I think that shows how much the family had been through.

That's right! Sheerah built Lower and Upper Beth-horon, and Uzzen-sheerah too. Three towns. In a list where most lines are just names, she gets a building permit. I've stamped a lot of cookies and never built a single town, so I'm impressed.

It's true, friend. The text says Sheerah "built Lower and Upper Beth-horon, as well as Uzzen-sheerah." That's three towns from one daughter. In a long list of names, she's the one with a construction résumé. Hard to beat that.

You got it, baker. The list ends with "Nun his son, and Joshua his son." This is the same Joshua who took over leading Israel after Moses died (Joshua 1:1-2). A long line of fathers and sons, and it lands on a name that matters. I'd have cheered if I could.

Caleb, a man from the tribe of Judah (Numbers 13:6), is a famous name from Joshua's day, so I see why he came to mind. But this verse says Nun's son is Joshua. Caleb isn't in this part of the list. Right neighborhood, friend, wrong house.
Gideon, a hero from the book of Judges (Judges 6:11), is a good name to know. He just isn't in this line. The verse says, "Nun his son, and Joshua his son." Joshua is the answer, friend.

That's right. Beriah and Shema were heads of families living in Aijalon. The same verse says they drove out the inhabitants of Gath. Settling down and pushing out the neighbors in one sentence. That's a busy verse.

Yes, Gath is the second blank. The verse says Beriah and Shema "drove out the inhabitants of Gath." That's the same city whose men killed Ephraim's sons earlier in the passage. I'll just let you notice that yourself.

Gibeon is in this passage, but later. It's where Jeiel, the father of Gibeon, lived with his wife Maacah (1 Chronicles 8:29). Beriah and Shema lived in Aijalon. Easy to mix up when the towns all start with G or A, friend.

Moab does show up in this chapter, because Shaharaim had sons there (1 Chronicles 8:8). But that's a different man in a different verse. For Beriah and Shema, the verse names Aijalon and Gath. Moab is the right chapter and the wrong family.

Geba is in the chapter too. Some heads of families lived there and were exiled to Manahath (1 Chronicles 8:6). But Beriah and Shema lived in Aijalon. That's a lot of towns to track, friend, and I'd lose my place too.

That's right. The verse says all these heads of families, the chiefs according to their genealogies, lived in Jerusalem. After all those towns and moves, a whole group lands in one city. A long list finally gets an address.
Hebron is a real city with real history. David ruled from there for a time (2 Samuel 2:11). But this verse says these chiefs lived in Jerusalem. Good guess, friend, wrong city.

Bethel does appear in this passage, as a holding of Joseph's descendants (1 Chronicles 7:28). But that's a different family from these Benjamite chiefs. This verse says they lived in Jerusalem. Right book, friend, different tribe's town.

That's it, baker. The text says, "Ner was the father of Kish, Kish was the father of Saul." This is the same Saul who became Israel's king (1 Samuel 11:15). After all those names, a familiar one finally walks in.

David was Jesse's son (1 Samuel 17:12), and he followed Saul as king. So he's in a different family line altogether. In this verse, Kish's son is Saul. Easy to swap them, since the two are so tied together in the story, friend.

Samuel was the prophet who anointed Saul (1 Samuel 10:1), so it makes sense he came to mind. But the text says, "Kish was the father of Saul." Samuel wasn't Kish's son. He's just close to the story, friend.

Yes. The verse says Saul was the father of "Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab, and Esh-baal." Jonathan is the first one named. Four sons in a row, and one name you probably know. I'd call that a good reading, baker.
It's true, friend. The verse says Saul was the father of "Jonathan, Malchishua, Abinadab, and Esh-baal." Jonathan is right there at the front. Four names, and he's the first one.
That's right. The verse says Ulam's sons were "mighty men of valor, archers." Add 150 sons and grandsons to that. That's a lot of bows in one family. I'd stay out of their backyard.
Charioteers would be a mighty sight, friend. But the verse doesn't mention chariots at all. It says Ulam's sons were "mighty men of valor, archers." Bows, not wheels.
Spearmen is a fair guess for a mighty family. But the verse says Ulam's sons were "mighty men of valor, archers." No spears are mentioned here. They're the ones with the bows, friend.
